In the context of large-scale structure cosmology, a cosmic speed field is defined as the velocity field of matter when considering a given moment in time. Despite being less directly connected to observable data compared to the cosmic web or density field, the speed field holds significant potential in mapping the underlying physics of the universe. To explore the speed field's capabilities in forecasting a dark matter halo's mass, we employed a deep learning approach, specifically a genetic algorithm to identify an optimal set of predictors among the speed field's Gaussian transformations. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that the speed field's lowest-order Gaussian transformation is highly correlated with halo masses, showcasing its potential in predicting a dark matter halo's mass through a neural network. To achieve this, we utilized a simulation known as EAGLE, consisting of $1000$ virtual galaxies with varying masses. Based on our findings, we constructed a neural network that forecasts a dark matter halo's mass more accurately than the speed field itself or its lowest-order Gaussian transformation. Furthermore, we observed that the speed field's lowest-order Gaussian transformation is closely related to the neural network's most important input components, aligning with our theoretical expectations regarding the speed field's performance in distinguishing different halo masses. To further validate our results, we applied the same deep learning strategy to real data from the DESI survey, utilizing a simulation known as DESi LightCone, consisting of $10^5$ virtual galaxies with varying masses, and achieved comparable outcomes. Ultimately, our results suggest that the speed field is capable of identifying halos based on their masses, leading to a clearer understanding of its performance in this role. To conclude, our research demonstrates that the cosmic speed field is effectively linked to the distribution of dark matter halo masses through a neural network, opening the possibility of employing the speed field in forecasting halo masses in surveys. Additionally, we contributed a code repository known as Speed4Halos for public use, available at https://github.com/Speed4Halos.
